risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the claim as worded (card sc_lopez_quintero_2011: JBI moderate; its printed pages and funding were checked against the version of record in 734_checks.json). A national probability sample with weights for non-response and one structured interview for every substance; but everything is self-reported, ages of first use and of dependence were recalled, sometimes decades later, the lifetime figures are actuarial projections without intervals, and people in institutions, and people who died, were deported, became impaired or went on military duty before the second interview, were not included. These limits would mostly lower the figures, which the statement gives as probably somewhat too low, and could not plausibly make dependence the usual outcome for cannabis, cocaine or alcohol. The nicotine lifetime figure and the timing figures (within 10 years, within the first year, the medians) rest most on the projection and on recalled ages; on their own they would be rated down one level, to very low, as in the answer on how many people who use cannabis become dependent. The predictors come from stepwise models whose covariates differ between substances, and are worded as associations.

inconsistency.note: One survey. The authors say its decade figures agree with an earlier national survey (Wagner & Anthony, 2002, not read), and its cannabis figure is close to that of the 1990–1992 survey described in the answer on cannabis dependence.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US household adults interviewed in 2001–2005, DSM-IV dependence on four substances, use defined as a first cigarette, drink or use; the statement says no figure here covers heroin or methamphetamine and names the measure.

imprecision.note: No interval is printed for any cumulative probability, but the estimates rest on 2,259 to 28,907 people who had used each substance, with 376 to 7,320 dependence cases in the models.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a national survey analysis.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive claim (cumulative probabilities in a survey population): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes), so low. Strict reading: the nicotine lifetime projection and the timing figures alone would be very low (risk of bias -1). Status single study: one survey, whose two waves are one study; the earlier national surveys mentioned are not anchored here and are not counted. Hart's two opinion pieces (narrative-review design on their cards) give no data and are used only for what he argues, beside the survey's figures, never as the source of a number; they do not enter the rating, and the comparison of his statements with the survey is the editors'. Heyman (2013) is used only for examples of the DSM-IV criteria. The predictors are associations from stepwise models and do not enter the rating of the probabilities.
rate.population: US civilian adults living in households and group quarters, interviewed in 2001–2002 and again in 2004–2005 (34,653 at both interviews; Black and Hispanic people and adults aged 18 to 24 oversampled; estimates weighted to the US population), in the subsamples who had ever used each substance (stated as 15,918 for nicotine, 28,907 for alcohol, 7,389 for cannabis and 2,259 for cocaine or crack)
rate.exposure: Ever having used the substance (a first full cigarette; at least one drink, not counting small tastes or sips; any cannabis; any cocaine or crack), from the recalled age of first use
rate.comparator: None for the probabilities (descriptive); for the predictors, people who had used the substance without the characteristic
rate.outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for dependence (three or more of seven within 12 months) at some time after first use, diagnosed by computer from a structured interview (AUDADIS-IV) with recalled ages of onset; cumulative probability by years since first use (actuarial survival estimates), and predictors as hazard ratios
rate.magnitude: Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), actuarial cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence among people who had ever used each substance (no intervals given): lifetime nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9%; 10 years after first use 15.6%, 11.0%, 14.8%, 5.9%; first year almost 2.0% (nicotine, alcohol, cannabis) and 7.1% (cocaine); half of the cases of dependence about 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after first use (a median among the people who became dependent). Stated subsamples 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259 (the rows of Tables 1 and 2 add to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263). Adjusted hazard ratios (Table 4), nicotine / alcohol / cannabis / cocaine: mood disorder 1.62 / 2.29 / 2.69 / 2.58; anxiety disorder 1.96 / 1.98 / 2.31 / not retained; personality disorder 1.42 / 1.64 / 2.3 / 1.99; dependence on another of the four substances 1.44 to 4.14. Unadjusted, lowest against highest individual income (Table 3): 1.39 / 1.23 / 2.77 / 2.76. Hart (2017, 2020): opinion pieces with no data; the range he states for heroin and methamphetamine is not used as a figure.
rate.short: Mostly not, except tobacco. In a big US survey, about 9 in 100 people who'd tried cannabis were expected to become dependent at some point. Cocaine 21, alcohol 23, tobacco 68.
rate.rate: One large US survey, done carefully, but built on memories, sometimes decades old. The lifetime figures are forecasts, the tobacco one most of all.

risk_of_bias.note: The human evidence is a case series (card sc_siegel_1984: JBI prevalence checklist, high risk): 10 survivors from one clinic, chosen in an unreported way, recalling the occasion about 5 years later in open-ended interviews, with the accounts sorted by the author without stated definitions or a second rater; with no comparison occasions and no comparison group, a count of 7 of 10 cannot estimate any risk. The one rat experiment read (card sc_siegel_1982: SYRCLE, high risk) reports no method of allocation, no blinding, no losses and no test statistics, and its printed p value for the main comparison does not reproduce from its counts; the other animal work is described by its author without figures (card sc_siegel_2005: a short narrative review of his own research programme, high risk).

inconsistency.note: No conflicting study was read; the author's own data include 3 of 10 who recalled nothing distinctive, which he reads as overdoses with a non-learned basis.

indirectness.note: The evidence that setting changes the chance of dying is from one rat experiment, which compared a heroin-paired setting with a familiar setting paired with an inactive injection (not a new place) and measured death, not tolerance; the human study interviewed survivors only, although its abstract extends the idea to deaths, and its unusual circumstances include changes of injection and of drug combination that the rat experiment did not test; the human laboratory examples concern alcohol and caffeine, not opioids or overdose.

imprecision.note: Ten people (7 of 10: exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation) and no comparison against which a risk could be estimated.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the 2005 review cites no study that failed to find setting-specific tolerance.

rate.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author's group: one rat experiment, read in full (Siegel et al., 1982), and other animal work described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005). In the rat experiment a high test dose killed about twice as many rats in the setting paired with an inactive injection as in the setting paired with heroin (27 of 42 against 12 of 37, editors' counts); both settings were familiar to every rat, death was the only outcome, tolerance was not measured, and the printed significance of the difference is overstated (p about .005 rather than < .001, editors' calculation). These findings show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings; they are not evidence about people, they concern a place linked with the drug rather than a new place, and they do not raise the rating. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 1982 experiment is in rats, and the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite the 1984 interviews).
rate.population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the one animal experiment read, 107 male Wistar-derived laboratory rats aged 90 to 110 days with no opioid experience at the start (37, 42 and 28 per group; editors' sum); in the other animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
rate.exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one); in the rat experiment, a single high intravenous heroin dose (15 mg/kg; study condition) given in the setting that had been paired with inactive dextrose injections, after 15 rising doses of heroin on alternate days in the other setting, both settings being familiar
rate.comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, rats with the same heroin history given the same test dose in the setting previously paired with heroin, and rats with no previous opioid that had had inactive injections in both settings
rate.outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in the rat experiment, death within minutes of a single high intravenous dose (tolerance itself not measured); in the review's other animal work, tolerance and death after a high dose
rate.magnitude: Siegel (1984): 7 of 10 survivors described the circumstances of the overdose occasion as unusual (70%; exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation): 2 injected in places where they had never injected before; 1 used in his own living room, where he had never taken heroin, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 took a barbiturate mixture with heroin against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without the cocaine he usually combined with it, for the first time in over 9 months; 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive feature. Unfamiliar place or company: 3 of 10 (editors' count). No comparison group, no comparison occasions, no test. Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982; 107 male rats, editors' sum; a single 15 mg/kg intravenous test dose after 15 rising doses on alternate days, study conditions): died after the test dose, heroin-paired setting 32.4% of 37 (12, editors' count), setting paired with an inactive dextrose injection 64.3% of 42 (27), controls with no previous opioid 96.4% of 28 (27); difference 31.9 percentage points, risk ratio 1.98 (Katz 95% CI 1.18 to 3.32), Pearson chi-square 7.98, p = 0.005 (continuity-corrected 6.76, p = 0.009; Fisher two-sided p = 0.007), against a printed P < .001 (editors' calculations); three groups printed P < .001 (chi-square 27.8, editors'), each heroin-experienced group against controls printed P < .002 (the closer one, 27 of 42 against 27 of 28: chi-square 9.8, p = 0.002, editors'); six of six replications in the same direction, printed P < .02 by a binomial test (one-sided 0.016, two-sided 0.031, editors'); median time from the start of the injection to death 187, 174 and 164 seconds, reported as not significantly different; test setting counterbalanced (17 and 20 of the 37; 21 and 21 of the 42, editors' arithmetic from 'half'), the two arrangements reported as not significantly different without numbers; no test statistics printed. Siegel (2005): no sample size or effect size for any study it cites.
rate.short: Maybe, but it's untested in people. In rats, a big dose killed 64 in 100 in a room not linked with heroin, and 32 in 100 in the heroin room.
rate.rate: One tiny study of 10 people's memories, with nobody to compare them with, plus one rat experiment that compared two familiar rooms. Rat findings don't show what happens in people.

risk_of_bias.note: The site counts come from 17 retrospective case series chosen by their own authors, 12 of them (75 of 127 people) for a particular site or presentation, added together with no weighting or interval in a review rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_nitro_2022); one group's three series hold 53 of the 127 and may share patients, as may the two series by Colletti et al.; and the review's counts for the Brescia series mix clinical with imaging findings and findings at presentation with findings during follow-up. The Brescia series is a referral series of severe cases with unclear selection, imaging in 16 of 18 read by one radiologist and several statistical errors (JBI prevalence checklist, high; card sc_trimarchi_2001). These could change the shares materially (for example the palate share, in series chosen for palatal holes), but not the finding that the septum was involved in nearly everyone with these lesions: one level. The course after stopping rests on the absence of follow-up data and on the opinion of one panel of rhinologists (card sc_saibene_2025: the project's narrative-review checklist, high), which the statement reports as opinion, not as evidence of an effect.

inconsistency.note: Septal perforation is reported in nearly every person of every series (review Table 3). The shares differ between the Brescia series and the pooled counts (a middle turbinate destroyed in 10 of 16 imaged, against 29 of 127 for the ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate), as expected from the Brescia series' selection of severe cases considered for a vasculitis; the statement gives both.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes people already diagnosed with these lesions who had come to doctors, says that how often snorting cocaine leads to them is unknown, gives the course after stopping as unstudied and the panel's statements as opinion. A reader asking what snorting does to their own nose needs the missing denominator, which the plain lines name as the main catch.

imprecision.note: 127 people pooled without intervals (editors' Wilson intervals, which overstate precision because the series are not one sample: palate 22.6% to 38.4%; eye socket or skull base 4.3% to 13.9%), with the deeper sites resting on 10 to 38 people; the comparison with Wegener granulomatosis on 18 against 21 people (16 imaged in each group); progression on 4 re-imaged people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review, which excluded case reports because they tend to describe extreme cases; the selective publication of striking or site-specific series is part of the selection counted under risk of bias and is not counted twice.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive claim (which structures were damaged in people already diagnosed, how the damage was told apart from a vasculitis in one series, what has and has not been studied about its course, and what one expert panel recommends): observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low (the arithmetic floors at very low); descriptive claims are never upgraded. The certainty concerns the description of published cases. It does not extend to how often snorting cocaine damages the nose, which no paper read measured, or to healing after stopping, which no paper read studied. The panel's statements on stopping, the 'safe threshold' and the 12-month wait before repair are opinion (a consensus without patient data, its search excluding the primary case series) and are reported as such; resting on them alone, the claim would stay at draft. Status replicated: septal perforation in nearly every person is reported in each of the 17 series, by 14 different first authors (review Tables 2 and 3); but the shares come from one review whose pool includes the Brescia series and two later series from the same group, so they are not independently replicated, and the comparison with Wegener granulomatosis and the repeat imaging rest on one series. The review and the consensus share their first and senior authors and are not independent of each other. The claim gives no advice on use; amounts that people reported in the Brescia series are left out because no paper related them to the damage.
rate.population: People who snort cocaine and have been diagnosed with cocaine-related destructive lesions of the nose or palate (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions), as described in published case series: 127 people in 17 retrospective series published 1989–2020 (61 men, 44 women, sex not given for 22; aged 22 to 66), 12 series of which (75 people) selected people for a particular site or presentation; in the one primary series read, 18 people seen in 1991–1999 in one otolaryngology department in Brescia, Italy (10 men, 8 women; aged 22 to 66, median 37; 16 imaged), all tested for a vasculitis; and, for the expert statements, a panel of 18 otolaryngologists (rhinologists under 45) from five countries in Europe and North America
rate.exposure: Snorting cocaine, as reported by the people themselves (17 of 18 in the Brescia series admitted it at the first visit; a reliable history of duration and amount could not be obtained for 7) or, in the consensus definition, shown by a drug test; where reported, 2 to 30 years of use; how often and how much people used, and whether they had stopped, were rarely reported and never related to the damage
rate.comparator: None for the site counts (people with lesions only; no people who snort cocaine without lesions); in the Brescia series, all 21 consecutive people with Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with nasal involvement biopsied in the same department and period (16 imaged); for the course of the lesions, repeat imaging in 4 people who kept using cocaine, and no one who had stopped
rate.outcome: Which structures were perforated, eroded or destroyed (clinical examination, endoscopy, CT or MRI); changes to the outside of the nose; infections; features telling the lesions apart from the vasculitis (symptoms elsewhere in the body, blood tests including ANCA, imaging, biopsies); progression on repeat imaging; the panel's agreement (ratings from 1 to 9) on definition, diagnosis, repair and the course after stopping
rate.magnitude: Nitro et al. (2022), 127 people with lesions in 17 series (Table 4; Fig. 2): septum 126 (99.2%); inferior turbinate or medial maxillary sinus wall 75 (59%); palate 38 (29.9%); ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate 29 (22.8%); lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base 10 (7.9%); counts per site, overlapping. Editors' Wilson 95% intervals treating the 127 as one sample, which overstates precision because the series were selected and differ: 95.7–99.9%, 50.4–67.2%, 22.6–38.4%, 16.4–30.9%, 4.3–13.9%. Series selecting a subgroup 12 of 17 (75 of 127 people); one group's three series 53 of 127 (editors' counts from Table 2). External nose (Table 5; 10 of 17 series): saddle nose 7 people in 5 series; nasal pyramid collapse 7 people in 2 series (editors' count). Use status known for 33 people: 18 using, 15 stopped (editors' count from Table 3); duration reported for 11 series (2–30 years), frequency for 2. Trimarchi et al. (2001), imaging at presentation, 16 of 18 people with lesions against 16 of 21 with Wegener granulomatosis (Table 3): septum 16 against 2; inferior turbinate 12 (both sides 9) against 0; middle turbinate 10 (both sides 5) against 0; superior turbinates 2; lateral nasal wall 5 (lamina papyracea 1); hard palate 4 (soft palate 1); 0 for each of these in the comparison group; second structure besides the septum 12 of 16 (75%) against 0 of 16; mean imaging score 4.06 (range 1–10) against 0.13 (0–1), p < 0.001. Figure 3 prints 61%, 33%, 16%, 11% and 28% for the inferior, middle and superior turbinates, the lateral wall and the floor or palate, which match neither. Palatal perforations 2 at the first visit, 5 by the end of follow-up (12–108 months, median 34). During follow-up: orbital infections 2, lung abscess 1, all resolved with antibiotics; S. aureus in the nose 15 of 17. Presentation, lesions against vasculitis (Table 1): fever 0 against 13; weight loss 0 against 7; arthralgia or arthritis 0 against 7; lung involvement 0 against 12; ear involvement 0 against 7; CRP 12.2 (SD 12) against 79.4 (73.7) mg/L, p = 0.002; ESR 31 (25) against 66 (41) mm/h, p = 0.009; abnormal CRP 9 of 18, ESR 8 of 18. Routine ANCA positive 13 of 18 against 19 of 21. Biopsies (Table 4): giant cells or granulomas 0 of 25 against 9 of 22; deep necrosis 0 of 25 against 19 of 22 (both p < 0.001); leukocytoclastic vasculitis 7 of 25 against 14 of 22 biopsies (p = 0.02), 6 of 18 against 9 of 21 people (printed p = 0.11; editors' Fisher exact p = 0.74). Repeat imaging: 4 people, 8 further examinations 7–52 months after the first, all still using, all progressed. Saibene et al. (2025), 18 panellists, ratings from 1 to 9 (mean; median; range; outliers; result): 1.1 definition 7.44; 7.5; 1–9; 1; consensus. 1.3 not relying on autoantibody tests 8.50; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.3 differential diagnoses 8.50; 9; 6–9; 1; consensus. 3.3 stopping the only known way to halt lesions 8.61; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 3.4 no safe threshold 8.89; 9; 8–9; 0; strong consensus. 4.7 repair only after toxicology-proven stopping covering at least 12 months 8.61; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus. 4.8 reconstruction techniques 7.94; 9; 4–9; 2; near-consensus. 3.15 palatal obturator first 8.11; 9; 3–9; 1; consensus. 2.13 full workup if lesions grow after reported stopping 8.56; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.14 drug test then 8.22; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus.
rate.short: It can make a hole in the wall between your nostrils, and damage can spread. 126 of 127 people with this damage had that hole. Healing after stopping hasn't been studied.
rate.rate: Reports of people who already had damage, often picked for one kind of problem, with no count of how many people who snort get it. Healing after stopping hasn't been studied; what experts say about it is opinion.

risk_of_bias.note: Coverage and measurement could change the figures materially (card sc_williams_2020, ROBINS-I serious): 3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped (30.5%) were excluded for losing Medicaid in the 6 months after stopping, a group that includes everyone who died; overdoses count only if billed to Medicaid; the printed code list leaves out the opioid codes, and the table of the codes used was not read.

inconsistency.note: One study; the four duration groups give similar overdose rates (5.1% to 5.5%).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Medicaid enrollees who stopped after at least 6 months and stayed enrolled; the statement says the figures leave out deaths, may not apply to people who stop early or are outside Medicaid, and come with no group that stayed on treatment.

imprecision.note: 464 overdoses; the overall share has a narrow interval (4.7% to 5.6%). The duration comparison for overdose is imprecise (0.75 to 1.44) and is worded as no detected difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; all four outcomes are reported for every comparison, including the null overdose result.

rate.reasoning: Descriptive (how many people had each event in the 6 months after stopping): starts low; down one level for risk of bias, because exclusions that include every death and an overdose definition that cannot be checked could change the figures materially: very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. The comparisons by length of treatment are associations in the same records, open to confounding by why and when people stopped, and are not rated separately; the authors concede the design cannot show cause. Nothing here compares stopping with continuing: deaths during and after treatment are the subject of the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine, which rests on a review of cohort studies and measures deaths, not treated overdoses; the two do not conflict. Status: single study.
rate.population: Adults aged 18 to 64 in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database (2013–2017; contributing states not named) who began a new buprenorphine episode for opioid use disorder, stayed on it continuously for 6 to 18 months, then stopped, and stayed enrolled in Medicaid for the 6 months afterwards: 8,996 people (61.0% women; 91.5% White; 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day); people also covered by Medicare were excluded
rate.exposure: Stopping buprenorphine (a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out) after 6–9 (4,126 people), 9–12 (2,440), 12–15 (1,499) or 15–18 months (931) of continuous treatment, by days supplied in pharmacy claims; the 6 months of follow-up counted from the last day of supply
rate.comparator: No group that continued buprenorphine. The longer-treatment groups against the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race (White or not), Medicaid plan type, recorded psychiatric, alcohol and other drug use disorder diagnoses, and starting dose
rate.outcome: At least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid (ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50), at least one emergency department visit, at least one inpatient admission, and at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription, in Medicaid claims in the 6 months after stopping; deaths not recorded
rate.magnitude: Williams et al. (2020). Flow: 26,576 with a new continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop (39.4%, editors) and 3,159 who stopped too late in the study window removed; 12,936 who stopped within the window; 3,940 (30.5%, editors) removed for incomplete enrolment in the 6 months after stopping; 8,996 analysed (6–9 months 4,126; 9–12 months 2,440; 12–15 months 1,499; 15–18 months 931). Six-month outcomes across the four groups, unadjusted: emergency department visit 41.2–48.6% (abstract 42.1–49.9%), inpatient admission 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescription 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdose 5.1–5.5%; overall overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6, editors). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% against 48.6% (p < 0.001), admissions 11.3% against 13.9% (p < 0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% against 25.9% (p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios against 6–9 months (Table 2): 15–18 months, admission 0.79 (0.64–0.99), emergency visit 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescription 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Overdose, other terms in the same model: women 0.65 (0.54–0.79); psychiatric diagnosis 1.61 (1.32–1.96); alcohol use disorder 2.02 (1.47–2.79); non-opioid drug use disorder 1.51 (1.22–1.86); starting dose 1.00 per mg (0.97–1.04). Sensitivity analysis (8,077 with a recorded opioid use disorder diagnosis): 15–18 against 6–9 months, emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); odds of overdose equivalent across groups, 5.6% overall.
rate.short: In US records, about 5 in 100 people had an overdose treated by a doctor within 6 months of stopping. Nearly half went to an emergency department.
rate.rate: One large study of insurance records. But people who died were left out, overdoses counted only if a doctor billed for them, and nobody who stayed on treatment was there to compare with.

risk_of_bias.note: The reviews' figures cannot be appraised: one author chose one study per cell with no stated search (card sc_verstraete_2004: high), and the clinical review's table comes from textbooks, laboratory web pages, a newsletter and older reviews (card sc_moeller_2017: high). In the primary study (card sc_goodwin_2008: JBI moderate), times run from admission rather than last use, and the last positive is cut off by the end of observation in 22 of the 54 people who ever screened positive; the statement words the averages as minimums, but the true times cannot be recovered, and the paper has internal inconsistencies (an impossible row; 4.3 against 4.6 days; a lowest group said to be all negative by eight days that includes one person positive at 21.8 days).

inconsistency.note: Figures differ widely between studies, drugs, fluids and cutoffs, but the differences follow the conditions the statement gives (single dose against heavy use, detection limit against cutoff, length of follow-up), and the direction agrees: days after a single dose, longer after heavy use, longest for cannabis.

indirectness.note: The question is how long drugs show on the tests people meet. The typical figures come from single, often low, controlled doses in a few volunteers, measured at laboratory detection limits (which give longer times than a screening cutoff, as the methamphetamine example shows) or at assorted cutoffs, and the clinical review's values carry no conditions at all. The primary study used one screening cutoff (50 ng/mL), counted from admission, and studied one selected US sample (77% men, 83% African American, paid, reporting dependence or abuse).

imprecision.note: Each table entry rests on one study, some of one or two people; the heroin percentages come without the numbers tested each day; in the primary study only 16 people were watched for 27 days or more, so the late part of the picture rests on few people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for narrative reviews or a single case series.

large_effect.note: A descriptive claim is not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: In the primary study, later last positives went with higher first-sample levels, but the groups were formed by that level and the fits are lines through three group means; not used.

rate.reasoning: Detection times are rated as descriptions (METHODS §6.3): the controlled-dose studies behind the reviews have no comparison group, and the primary study is a case series; start low. Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 (see the domain notes) take it to very low, the floor. The figures from the two narrative reviews are second-hand and the statement says so; the 2004 review reports the numbers of the primary studies it summarizes, which is the only way they are seen here. The one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008) is the strongest evidence for cannabis because abstinence was enforced, so later positive screens reflect what was left in the body, not new use; but it cannot give detection times from last use, and its averages are minimums. Status replicated: the direction (days after a single dose; longer, up to weeks, after heavy regular use, most of all for cannabis) agrees across separate studies described in the reviews (for cannabis, single-cigarette studies and a detoxification ward of 52 people) and the primary study; but every specific figure rests on one study, and only one primary study was read. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.
rate.population: People tested for drugs after use: in the studies summarized second-hand by two narrative reviews, mostly healthy volunteers given a single controlled dose (some studies of one or two people) and people who stopped regular use in prison, on a detoxification ward or on a closed research unit; in the one primary study read, 60 adults aged 18 to 45 in the USA (46 men, 14 women; 50 African American; mean age 26.9) who reported cannabis dependence or abuse (DSM-IV terms) and smoking on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days, kept abstinent on a closed research unit
rate.exposure: Last use of a drug, as a single controlled dose given by researchers or as the end of regular use (in prison, on a detoxification ward or on admission to a closed research unit), followed by tests of urine, blood, oral fluid or hair; in the primary study, cannabis smoked before admission (amounts and THC content unknown; days since last use not reported), then enforced abstinence for up to 30 days
rate.comparator: None: detection times are described, not compared with a control group; in some reviewed studies the same samples were read at different limits or cutoffs; in the primary study, groups formed by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first urine sample
rate.outcome: Detection time: how long after a single dose, after last reported use or after admission a drug or its breakdown product was found above the stated detection limit or cutoff; in the primary study, days from admission to the first negative and to the last positive urine screen at 50 ng/mL, and whether people were still screening positive when observation ended

item.statement: Most people who try cocaine become dependent on it.
item.why: In a big US survey, about 21 in 100 people who had tried cocaine were expected to become dependent at some point. The figures rest on people's own memories.

lines.short: Mostly not, except tobacco. In a big US survey, about 9 in 100 people who'd tried cannabis were expected to become dependent at some point. Cocaine 21, alcohol 23, tobacco 68.
lines.but: It's people's own memories, in one US survey from 2001 to 2005. People in prison, or who had died, weren't asked, so the real figures may be higher.
how: Dependence meant at least 3 of 7 signs in the same year, like needing more for the same effect, withdrawal, or not managing to stop. It came from people's answers, not tests.
For cannabis and cocaine it often came early: half of those who became dependent did so within about 4 to 5 years of first use. For alcohol it took 13 years, for tobacco 27.
People with depression, anxiety or another dependence became dependent more often. That's a link, not proof of a cause.

Drug researcher Carl Hart says most people who use drugs never get addicted. His opinion pieces give no data. The survey fits that for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol, not tobacco. It has no figures for heroin or meth.

item.statement: In the rat study, heroin was deadlier in a room the rats had never seen.
item.why: Every rat knew both rooms. Heroin killed about 64 in 100 rats in the room linked with dummy injections, against 32 in 100 in the room linked with heroin. Rats aren't people.

lines.short: Maybe, but it's untested in people. In rats, a big dose killed 64 in 100 in a room not linked with heroin, and 32 in 100 in the heroin room.
lines.but: The rats knew both rooms, so it wasn't a new place. In people, there's just one study: 10 survivors' memories, with nobody to compare.
how: The idea: the place, people and ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance. So it may be weaker where the drug isn't usually taken.

In the rat study, each rat had heroin in one room and dummy injections of sugar water in the other. A big dose then killed about 64 in 100 rats in the dummy room, 32 in 100 in the heroin room, and 96 in 100 rats that had never had heroin.
Nobody measured the rats' tolerance, only whether they died. The paper also overstated how sure its result was, though more rats died in the dummy room in all six repeats. Rats aren't people.

In people, 10 overdose survivors were asked what was different that day. 7 recalled something unusual: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new with no overdose.

item.statement: Studies show a hole in the nose from snorting closes up once you stop.
item.why: None of these studies followed people after they stopped. Experts think stopping is the only known way to halt the damage, but that's opinion.

lines.short: It can make a hole in the wall between your nostrils, and damage can spread. 126 of 127 people with this damage had that hole. Healing after stopping hasn't been studied.
lines.but: These are people who already had damage and went to doctors. Nobody knows how many people who snort get it.
how: 17 published case series held 127 people with this damage. 126 had a hole in the septum, the wall between the nostrils. Fewer had damage further in: about 59 in 100 on the lower side walls, 30 in 100 in the roof of the mouth, 23 in 100 higher up, 8 in 100 at the eye socket or skull base.

It can look like a disease that inflames blood vessels. In one Italian clinic, a blood test for that disease was positive in 13 of 18 people with cocaine damage, and some were first treated for that disease, which didn't help. Unlike many with that disease, none of the 18 had fever or illness elsewhere in the body.

None of these studies followed people after they stopped. In the Italian clinic, 4 people were scanned again months or years later. All 4 had kept using cocaine, and all had more damage. In one, it reached the base of the skull within three years.

18 nose doctors agreed, as opinion, that stopping is the only known way to halt the damage. They said no amount of use is safe for it. They'd wait for drug tests showing 12 months off cocaine before repair surgery.

item.statement: In one US study, about 5 in 100 had a doctor treat an overdose within 6 months of stopping Suboxone.
item.why: 464 of 8,996 people on Medicaid who stopped after 6 to 18 months did. People who died were left out, so fatal overdoses aren't counted.

lines.short: In US records, about 5 in 100 people had an overdose treated by a doctor within 6 months of stopping. Nearly half went to an emergency department.
lines.but: People who died were left out, so fatal overdoses aren't counted. And nobody stayed on Suboxone to compare with.
how: US public health insurance (Medicaid) records tracked 8,996 people for 6 months after they stopped Suboxone's main drug, buprenorphine. They'd been on it for 6 to 18 months.

464 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor (5 in 100). 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid.
People who'd been on it 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than those who stopped at 6 to 9 months. Their overdoses were no fewer.
Anyone who died or lost Medicaid in those 6 months was left out, and the records don't say why people stopped. Deaths during and after treatment are in a separate answer.

item.why: Each figure in one review came from one small study, some of just one or two people given one dose. Another chart came from textbooks, older reviews and lab websites.

how: One expert review sums up: after one use, most drugs showed in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 to 2 days and in saliva for up to 2 days.

Each figure came from one small study, often measured to a lab's lowest limit. Another chart came from textbooks, older reviews and lab websites. The limit matters: one dose of meth showed for 87 hours at a lab's limit, 43 at a higher cutoff.

On a locked ward where nobody could smoke, 60 regular weed smokers were tested for up to 30 days. 13 of the 20 with the highest levels were still positive when testing ended. Positives often came back after a negative.

item.statement: Indica and sativa labels tell you which smell compounds your weed has.
item.why: In 41,201 US lab-tested samples, the labels barely matched the mix of smell compounds (terpenes). The labels came from a strain website, not the bags, and effects weren't measured.

lines.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
lines.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed made people feel.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples from licensed growers in six US states, 2013 to 2021. In every state, 94 to 97 in 100 samples had at least five times as much THC as CBD. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name, and weren't compared on THC or CBD.

In 41,201 samples where THC outweighed CBD, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.
