lines.statement: In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again in 2004–2005 (the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions; 34,653 people at both interviews), the estimated chance of ever becoming dependent was well under one in two for people who had used cannabis, cocaine or alcohol, and about two in three for people who had ever smoked a full cigarette. Among people who had ever used each substance (stated as 7,389 for cannabis, 2,259 for cocaine or crack, 28,907 for alcohol and 15,918 for nicotine), the estimated probability of meeting DSM-IV criteria for dependence at some time in life was 8.9% for cannabis, 20.9% for cocaine, 22.7% for alcohol and 67.5% for nicotine; within 10 years of first use it was 5.9%, 14.8%, 11.0% and 15.6%, and within the first year almost 2% for cannabis, alcohol and nicotine and 7.1% for cocaine. Among the people who became dependent, half had done so within about 4 years of first using cocaine, 5 years for cannabis, 13 for alcohol and 27 for nicotine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). Dependence meant three or more of seven DSM-IV criteria within the same 12 months (signs such as tolerance, withdrawal, using more than intended or failing to stop after resolving to; Heyman, 2013), diagnosed by computer from answers to a structured interview; use meant a first full cigarette, at least one drink not counting sips, or any use of cannabis or of cocaine or crack. These are survey reports: everything rests on what people said, without tests, and on ages they recalled, sometimes decades later; the lifetime figures are projections from survival curves that join younger and older people's histories, and no interval is given for any of them; and the survey left out people living in institutions such as prisons, who the authors say are more likely to have a dependence diagnosis, and, at the second interview, people who had died, been deported, become too impaired to take part or gone on active military duty, so the figures are probably somewhat too low (editors' inference). In the adjusted models, dependence was more likely among people with a mood, anxiety or personality disorder or with dependence on another substance (hazard ratios 1.42 to 4.14), associations that cannot show cause; in the same models neither education nor income predicted dependence, although lower individual income went with it before adjustment (hazard ratios up to 2.77 for cannabis and 2.76 for cocaine, lowest against highest income band) and income could not be modelled as changing over time. Carl Hart, a Columbia University professor of psychology and psychiatry who studies drug effects in people, argues in a one-page opinion piece, without numbers or sources, that the vast majority of people who use cocaine and other recreational drugs never become addicted and that among the relatively few who do, co-occurring psychiatric disorders and socioeconomic factors account for a substantial share (Hart, 2017); in a second opinion piece he states that 70% to 90% of people who use even heroin or methamphetamine do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder, citing only his own book and giving no survey, year or definition (Hart, 2020). The survey's estimates fit his first statement for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol but not for nicotine, and no survey read here gives a figure for heroin or methamphetamine, so his range cannot be checked against them (editors' comparison). An earlier US survey (1990–1992), whose figures count dependence by the time of the interview rather than over a projected lifetime and include heroin, is described in the answer on how many people who use cannabis become dependent; how often people stop meeting the criteria is the answer on recovery from drug or alcohol problems. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: US civilian adults living in households and group quarters, interviewed in 2001–2002 and again in 2004–2005 (34,653 at both interviews; Black and Hispanic people and adults aged 18 to 24 oversampled; estimates weighted to the US population), in the subsamples who had ever used each substance (stated as 15,918 for nicotine, 28,907 for alcohol, 7,389 for cannabis and 2,259 for cocaine or crack)
lines.exposure: Ever having used the substance (a first full cigarette; at least one drink, not counting small tastes or sips; any cannabis; any cocaine or crack), from the recalled age of first use
lines.comparator: None for the probabilities (descriptive); for the predictors, people who had used the substance without the characteristic
lines.outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for dependence (three or more of seven within 12 months) at some time after first use, diagnosed by computer from a structured interview (AUDADIS-IV) with recalled ages of onset; cumulative probability by years since first use (actuarial survival estimates), and predictors as hazard ratios
lines.magnitude: Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), actuarial cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence among people who had ever used each substance (no intervals given): lifetime nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9%; 10 years after first use 15.6%, 11.0%, 14.8%, 5.9%; first year almost 2.0% (nicotine, alcohol, cannabis) and 7.1% (cocaine); half of the cases of dependence about 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after first use (a median among the people who became dependent). Stated subsamples 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259 (the rows of Tables 1 and 2 add to 16,053, 29,160, 7,409 and 2,263). Adjusted hazard ratios (Table 4), nicotine / alcohol / cannabis / cocaine: mood disorder 1.62 / 2.29 / 2.69 / 2.58; anxiety disorder 1.96 / 1.98 / 2.31 / not retained; personality disorder 1.42 / 1.64 / 2.3 / 1.99; dependence on another of the four substances 1.44 to 4.14. Unadjusted, lowest against highest individual income (Table 3): 1.39 / 1.23 / 2.77 / 2.76. Hart (2017, 2020): opinion pieces with no data; the range he states for heroin and methamphetamine is not used as a figure.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive claim (cumulative probabilities in a survey population): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS 6.3); not downgraded (see the domain notes), so low. Strict reading: the nicotine lifetime projection and the timing figures alone would be very low (risk of bias -1). Status single study: one survey, whose two waves are one study; the earlier national surveys mentioned are not anchored here and are not counted. Hart's two opinion pieces (narrative-review design on their cards) give no data and are used only for what he argues, beside the survey's figures, never as the source of a number; they do not enter the rating, and the comparison of his statements with the survey is the editors'. Heyman (2013) is used only for examples of the DSM-IV criteria. The predictors are associations from stepwise models and do not enter the rating of the probabilities.

lines.q: Do most people who try drugs get addicted?
lines.short: Mostly not, except tobacco. In a big US survey, about 9 in 100 people who'd tried cannabis were expected to become dependent at some point. Cocaine 21, alcohol 23, tobacco 68.
lines.but: It's people's own memories, in one US survey from 2001 to 2005. People in prison, or who had died, weren't asked, so the real figures may be higher.
how: Dependence meant at least 3 of 7 signs in the same year, like needing more for the same effect, withdrawal, or not managing to stop. It came from people's answers, not tests.
For cannabis and cocaine it often came early: half of those who became dependent did so within about 4 to 5 years of first use. For alcohol it took 13 years, for tobacco 27.
People with depression, anxiety or another dependence became dependent more often. That's a link, not proof of a cause.

Drug researcher Carl Hart says most people who use drugs never get addicted. His opinion pieces give no data. The survey fits that for cannabis, cocaine and alcohol, not tobacco. It has no figures for heroin or meth.

lines.statement: In people who use heroin, evidence is insufficient to say whether taking it in surroundings not linked with past use raises the risk of overdose: the idea comes from a conditioning model of tolerance tested mainly in rats, and the only study in people is a set of 10 overdose survivors' recollections with no comparison. The model, as its author states it (Siegel, 1984, 2005): cues present when a drug is taken, such as the place, the people and the act of taking it, become linked with its effects and come to trigger responses that oppose those effects; these learned responses are part of tolerance, so tolerance should be weaker where the drug has not been taken before. The one animal experiment read is in rats (Siegel et al., 1982): male laboratory rats were given 15 intravenous heroin injections in rising amounts, one every other day, always in one of two settings (the colony room, where each was housed alone, or a separate room with constant white noise), and an inactive injection of dextrose solution in the other setting on the days between, so both settings were familiar to every rat; each rat then had one high test dose (15 mg/kg; study condition) either in the setting paired with heroin or in the setting paired with the inactive injection, and death within minutes, judged by the absence of a heartbeat, was the only outcome. In the heroin-paired setting 32.4% of 37 rats died, in the setting paired with the inactive injection 64.3% of 42, and among 28 control rats that had never had an opioid 96.4% (editors' counts from the printed percentages, each of which fits only one whole number: 12 of 37, 27 of 42 and 27 of 28; a difference of about 32 in 100 and a risk ratio of about 2.0, 95% CI 1.2 to 3.3, editors' calculation), and in each of six replications more rats died in the setting paired with the inactive injection. The experiment therefore compared a place linked with the drug with a familiar place linked with an inactive injection, not a familiar place with a new one; tolerance itself was never measured, so weaker tolerance as the reason is the authors' interpretation; and the paper names no method of assigning rats to groups, reports no losses and prints no test statistics, and its p < .001 for the difference between the two heroin-experienced groups does not reproduce from its own counts (chi-square about 8.0, p about .005, editors' calculation). Setting-specific tolerance is also said to have been seen for a variety of effects, lethal effects included, of various drugs in many species (Siegel, 2005, citing his group's 2000 review, with no study, species or figure named). The 2005 review also describes, without numbers, two laboratory examples in people that do not involve opioids: more tolerance to alcohol drunk in a familiar beer-flavoured drink than in an unfamiliar blue, peppermint-flavoured one, and more tolerance to a heart effect of caffeine taken in coffee than at the same blood level reached intravenously. The only human study of overdose: 10 people formerly dependent on heroin (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28), attending one methadone maintenance clinic in the New York City area and each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records, were asked to recount the occasion on average 5 years later; 7 described something unusual: 2 had injected in places where they had never injected before, 1 had used for the first time in his own living room, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply, 2 described an unusual injection, 1 had taken a barbiturate mixture with the heroin against his usual practice, and 1 had injected heroin without the cocaine he usually took with it; 3 recalled nothing distinctive (Siegel, 1984). An unfamiliar place or company was thus recalled by 3 of the 10 (editors' count). There was no comparison with these people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose, the accounts were sorted by the author without stated definitions, and only survivors were interviewed, although the abstract extends the suggestion to overdose deaths; the author states that the reports do not prove a conditioning mechanism, that large doses and drug combinations also contribute, that the barbiturate case may be a drug interaction, and that how often people use heroin in unusual circumstances without harm is unknown. The 2005 review presents no data on overdose in people and does not cite the interviews; it proposes a form of cue-exposure treatment (meeting drug cues without the drug, so that the learned responses fade) that also includes internal cues, and cites no trial of it. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who use heroin: in the only human study, 10 people formerly dependent on heroin, in methadone maintenance at one clinic in the New York City area, each with a hospital admission for overdose in their records (8 men, 2 women; mean age 28 at interview), interviewed on average 5 years after the overdose; in the one animal experiment read, 107 male Wistar-derived laboratory rats aged 90 to 110 days with no opioid experience at the start (37, 42 and 28 per group; editors' sum); in the other animal work the model's author describes, rats and other species
lines.exposure: Taking an opioid in surroundings, company or circumstances not previously linked with taking it (in the human study, anything the person recalled as unusual on the overdose occasion: an unfamiliar place or company, an unusual injection, an unusual drug combination or the absence of a usual one); in the rat experiment, a single high intravenous heroin dose (15 mg/kg; study condition) given in the setting that had been paired with inactive dextrose injections, after 15 rising doses of heroin on alternate days in the other setting, both settings being familiar
lines.comparator: None in the human study (no comparison with the same people's ordinary occasions of use or with people who did not overdose); in the rat experiment, rats with the same heroin history given the same test dose in the setting previously paired with heroin, and rats with no previous opioid that had had inactive injections in both settings
lines.outcome: Overdose (hospital-treated, survivors only) in people; in the rat experiment, death within minutes of a single high intravenous dose (tolerance itself not measured); in the review's other animal work, tolerance and death after a high dose
lines.magnitude: Siegel (1984): 7 of 10 survivors described the circumstances of the overdose occasion as unusual (70%; exact 95% CI 35% to 93%, editors' calculation): 2 injected in places where they had never injected before; 1 used in his own living room, where he had never taken heroin, with a large group at his wedding celebration, and alone overdosed from the shared supply; 2 described unusual injection procedures; 1 took a barbiturate mixture with heroin against his usual practice; 1 injected heroin without the cocaine he usually combined with it, for the first time in over 9 months; 3 of 10 recalled no distinctive feature. Unfamiliar place or company: 3 of 10 (editors' count). No comparison group, no comparison occasions, no test. Rat experiment (Siegel et al., 1982; 107 male rats, editors' sum; a single 15 mg/kg intravenous test dose after 15 rising doses on alternate days, study conditions): died after the test dose, heroin-paired setting 32.4% of 37 (12, editors' count), setting paired with an inactive dextrose injection 64.3% of 42 (27), controls with no previous opioid 96.4% of 28 (27); difference 31.9 percentage points, risk ratio 1.98 (Katz 95% CI 1.18 to 3.32), Pearson chi-square 7.98, p = 0.005 (continuity-corrected 6.76, p = 0.009; Fisher two-sided p = 0.007), against a printed P < .001 (editors' calculations); three groups printed P < .001 (chi-square 27.8, editors'), each heroin-experienced group against controls printed P < .002 (the closer one, 27 of 42 against 27 of 28: chi-square 9.8, p = 0.002, editors'); six of six replications in the same direction, printed P < .02 by a binomial test (one-sided 0.016, two-sided 0.031, editors'); median time from the start of the injection to death 187, 174 and 164 seconds, reported as not significantly different; test setting counterbalanced (17 and 20 of the 37; 21 and 21 of the 42, editors' arithmetic from 'half'), the two arrangements reported as not significantly different without numbers; no test statistics printed. Siegel (2005): no sample size or effect size for any study it cites.
lines.reasoning: The only human evidence on overdose and setting is a case series of 10 survivors' recollections with no comparison (Siegel, 1984): observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision; very low. The model and the animal findings come from the same author's group: one rat experiment, read in full (Siegel et al., 1982), and other animal work described without figures in a short narrative review (Siegel, 2005). In the rat experiment a high test dose killed about twice as many rats in the setting paired with an inactive injection as in the setting paired with heroin (27 of 42 against 12 of 37, editors' counts); both settings were familiar to every rat, death was the only outcome, tolerance was not measured, and the printed significance of the difference is overstated (p about .005 rather than < .001, editors' calculation). These findings show why the idea is plausible and are labelled as animal findings; they are not evidence about people, they concern a place linked with the drug rather than a new place, and they do not raise the rating. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study of people compared overdose occasions with ordinary ones. Status: single study (one human study; the 1982 experiment is in rats, and the 2005 review adds no human overdose data and does not cite the 1984 interviews).

lines.q: Can using in a new place make an overdose more likely?
lines.short: Maybe, but it's untested in people. In rats, a big dose killed 64 in 100 in a room not linked with heroin, and 32 in 100 in the heroin room.
lines.but: The rats knew both rooms, so it wasn't a new place. In people, there's just one study: 10 survivors' memories, with nobody to compare.
how: The idea: the place, people and ritual that come with a drug start to trigger the body's push-back against it. That push-back is part of tolerance. So it may be weaker where the drug isn't usually taken.

In the rat study, each rat had heroin in one room and dummy injections of sugar water in the other. A big dose then killed about 64 in 100 rats in the dummy room, 32 in 100 in the heroin room, and 96 in 100 rats that had never had heroin.
Nobody measured the rats' tolerance, only whether they died. The paper also overstated how sure its result was, though more rats died in the dummy room in all six repeats. Rats aren't people.

In people, 10 overdose survivors were asked what was different that day. 7 recalled something unusual: 3 a new place or crowd, 2 a different way of injecting, 2 a different mix of drugs. Nobody counted how often people use somewhere new with no overdose.

lines.statement: In people who snort cocaine and have been diagnosed with cocaine-related destruction of the nose and palate (in the papers, cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions), the damage described ranges from a hole in the nasal septum, which nearly all of them had, to destruction of the turbinates, the side walls of the nose and the palate and, less often, of the walls of the eye socket and the skull base. How many people who snort cocaine develop such damage is not known, because every study read counted only people who already had it and had come to doctors; and whether the damage stops or heals after cocaine use stops has not been studied, since no series in the systematic review (published in 2022) and no paper read followed people after they stopped. In 17 retrospective case series published from 1989 to 2020 and gathered by a systematic review (127 people with these lesions among 282 participants; 61 men and 44 women, sex not given for 22; aged 22 to 66), the septum was involved in 126 people (99.2%), the inferior turbinate or the inner wall of the maxillary sinus in 75 (59%), the palate in 38 (29.9%), the ethmoid or the middle or superior turbinate in 29 (22.8%), and the thin bone between the nose and the eye socket (lamina papyracea), the eye socket itself or the skull base in 10 (7.9%) (Nitro et al., 2022, Table 4 and Figure 2; the abstract and results text give the 59% and the 29.9% to the nasal floor and the lower side wall instead, which leaves out the palate). These are counts at one time, added across series of which 12 (75 of the 127 people) studied people chosen for a particular site or presentation, such as a hole in the palate or a picture resembling vasculitis (editors' count from Table 2). Series from the same groups may share patients (three from one Italian group hold 53 of the 127; editors' count), which the review does not address, and for the Italian series of 2001 the review's counts mix clinical with imaging findings and include palatal holes and eye-socket infections that appeared only during follow-up (editors' comparison of the review's Table 3 with the primary paper). Changes to the outside of the nose, such as a sunken bridge (saddle nose, 7 people in 5 series) or a collapsed nose (7 people in 2 series by one team), were listed for 10 of the 17 series; the others did not report on the outside of the nose, so no share can be given. Where reported, people had used cocaine for 2 to 30 years; how long, how often and how much they had used, and whether they had stopped (known for 33 of the 127: 18 still using, 15 stopped; editors' count from Table 3), were too sparsely reported to relate to the damage. The review proposes that the damage starts at the septum and spreads to the lower, then the middle parts of the nose and only then to the eye socket and skull base; this is a hypothesis drawn from the counts, which the authors say needs prospective validation, describing the sparse data over time in one series (Trimarchi et al., 2003, not read) as seeming to fit it. Of 18 people seen in the otolaryngology department in Brescia, Italy, from 1991 to 1999 (10 men and 8 women aged 22 to 66; 17 admitted cocaine use at the first visit; followed for 12 to 108 months), all came with long-standing symptoms such as a blocked nose, nosebleeds or facial pain, and the commonest findings were widespread ulcers with dead tissue, extensive crusting and a hole in the septum; holes in the palate were present in 2 people at the first visit and appeared in 3 more during follow-up, with trouble swallowing and food or drink passing into the nose. On imaging at presentation (16 people), all had a septal hole, 12 had at least partial destruction of an inferior turbinate (both sides in 9), 10 of a middle turbinate, 2 erosion of the superior turbinates, 5 erosion of the side wall of the nose (reaching the lamina papyracea in 1) and 4 erosion of the floor of the nose, the hard palate; these counts come from the text and Table 3, because the paper's Figure 3 prints percentages that match neither (for example 61% for the inferior turbinate, against 12 of 16). During follow-up 2 people with severe destruction developed infections spreading from the nose into the eye socket and 1 a Staphylococcus aureus lung abscess, all of which cleared with antibiotics; 15 of 17 tested had S. aureus in the nose (Trimarchi et al., 2001). The papers explain the damage, without testing it and citing earlier work, mainly by cocaine narrowing the blood vessels of the nasal lining so that tissue dies, with possible parts played by substances mixed into the cocaine (such as levamisole; see the answer on levamisole), the force of the inhaled powder and repeated infection; milder changes (a stuffy nose, headache, a weaker sense of smell) are mentioned only as background in one paper, with no count of how often they occur. The damage can look like other diseases that destroy the middle of the face, among them granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis, a vasculitis), sarcoidosis and nasal lymphoma; older criteria described by the review suspected the condition when two of a septal hole, a palatal hole and destruction of the side wall were present, with other diagnoses ruled out and a drug screen (Seyer et al., as described by Nitro et al., 2022). The consensus panel's list of conditions to rule out also includes infections such as syphilis, leishmaniasis, leprosy and tuberculosis, Crohn's disease, long-term use of vessel-narrowing (decongestant) drugs, nose picking, injury, snorting other drugs and IgG4-related disease (Saibene et al., 2025, statement 2.3). In the Brescia comparison with all 21 people with Wegener granulomatosis and nasal involvement biopsied there in the same years, none of the 18 people with cocaine lesions had fever, weight loss, joint pain, or lung or ear involvement at presentation (13, 7, 7, 12 and 7 of the 21 had); markers of inflammation in the blood were lower on average (CRP 12.2 against 79.4 mg/L; ESR 31 against 66 mm/h), although CRP was abnormal in 9 and ESR in 8 of the 18, which the conclusion's statement that signs of systemic inflammation were absent in all does not fit; on imaging, the septum was perforated in 16 of 16 against 2 of 16, and structures beyond it were destroyed in 12 of 16 against none; routine ANCA blood tests, used to diagnose the vasculitis, were positive in 13 of 18 (19 of 21 in the comparison group), and some people with cocaine lesions were first treated as for the vasculitis, with cytotoxic drugs, without benefit; and in biopsies, changes in vessel walls were found in both diseases, but granulomas or giant cells (0 of 25 abnormal biopsies, against 9 of 22) and deep areas of dead tissue (0 of 25, against 19 of 22) only in the vasculitis. The authors say referral bias may explain part of these differences, since people with cocaine lesions may come to a doctor only after much damage. The consensus panel agreed that the diagnosis should not rest on autoantibody tests such as ANCA (statement 1.3, strong consensus) and defined the condition as any structural lesion of the nose and sinuses in a person whose cocaine snorting is confirmed by their own account or by a drug test (1.1, consensus, the lowest-rated statement adopted), a one-lesion definition it presents as replacing older ones. No series in the review reported what happened to the lesions after people stopped (use status was not reported for the one series with some data over time), and the only repeat imaging in the papers read is of 4 people in the Brescia series, all of whom said they had kept using cocaine and all of whom had further destruction on scans 7 to 52 months after the first; in one of them, over three years, it reached the whole framework of the nose, the hard and soft palate and the central floor of the front of the skull base, with brain tissue bulging through the gap (a meningoencephalocele). In the 2025 consensus (18 otolaryngologists under 45 from the rhinology research group of the young otolaryngologists' section of the International Federation of Otorhinolaryngological Societies, in five countries in Europe and North America, all of them authors, rating 44 statements from 1 to 9 over three anonymous rounds, rewording those short of consensus; strong consensus means a mean of at least 8 with no rating 2 or more points from it), the panel agreed that people with these lesions must be told that stopping snorting cocaine is the only known way to halt them (statement 3.3, strong consensus, mean 8.61) and that no 'safe threshold' of cocaine use keeps them from progressing (3.4, the highest-rated statement, mean 8.89), both supported in its discussion by a single cited paper (Trimarchi et al., 2014, not read); that repair of the septum, nose or palate should not be done unless the person is motivated and shows, by toxicology covering at least 12 months, that they have stopped (4.7, consensus, mean 8.61, one outlier), a period taken from the DSM-5 definition of sustained remission, with an uncited remark that the risk of relapse falls the longer abstinence lasts, rather than from any data on healing; that a plate covering the hole (an obturator prosthesis) can be offered first for a hole in the palate (3.15, consensus); and that lesions that grow after a person reports stopping call for a full workup for other causes, in which a drug test can be considered (2.13, strong consensus; 2.14, consensus). Repair techniques reached only near-consensus (4.8), the literature on them being described as anecdotal. The discussion describes a septal hole that has settled, with no crusting or inflammation, in someone who used cocaine in earlier years but not recently, as fitting cocaine damage, and crusting or inflammation then as a reason to look for another cause; no paper gives data on how often, or how fast, lesions settle, stay the same or grow after stopping. These statements are expert opinion: the panel's literature search kept only reviews and higher-level designs (23 articles, plus one the panel added), most of them, by the authors' account, descriptive studies without a control group; no statement carries a grade of its evidence; the review's first and senior authors were among the panel's three leaders, and the panel adopted the review's four-grade scale (statement 2.2); and only rhinologists voted, with no specialist in drug-use treatment and no person who uses cocaine, although the abstract calls the panel multidisciplinary. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People who snort cocaine and have been diagnosed with cocaine-related destructive lesions of the nose or palate (cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions), as described in published case series: 127 people in 17 retrospective series published 1989–2020 (61 men, 44 women, sex not given for 22; aged 22 to 66), 12 series of which (75 people) selected people for a particular site or presentation; in the one primary series read, 18 people seen in 1991–1999 in one otolaryngology department in Brescia, Italy (10 men, 8 women; aged 22 to 66, median 37; 16 imaged), all tested for a vasculitis; and, for the expert statements, a panel of 18 otolaryngologists (rhinologists under 45) from five countries in Europe and North America
lines.exposure: Snorting cocaine, as reported by the people themselves (17 of 18 in the Brescia series admitted it at the first visit; a reliable history of duration and amount could not be obtained for 7) or, in the consensus definition, shown by a drug test; where reported, 2 to 30 years of use; how often and how much people used, and whether they had stopped, were rarely reported and never related to the damage
lines.comparator: None for the site counts (people with lesions only; no people who snort cocaine without lesions); in the Brescia series, all 21 consecutive people with Wegener granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with nasal involvement biopsied in the same department and period (16 imaged); for the course of the lesions, repeat imaging in 4 people who kept using cocaine, and no one who had stopped
lines.outcome: Which structures were perforated, eroded or destroyed (clinical examination, endoscopy, CT or MRI); changes to the outside of the nose; infections; features telling the lesions apart from the vasculitis (symptoms elsewhere in the body, blood tests including ANCA, imaging, biopsies); progression on repeat imaging; the panel's agreement (ratings from 1 to 9) on definition, diagnosis, repair and the course after stopping
lines.magnitude: Nitro et al. (2022), 127 people with lesions in 17 series (Table 4; Fig. 2): septum 126 (99.2%); inferior turbinate or medial maxillary sinus wall 75 (59%); palate 38 (29.9%); ethmoid, middle or superior turbinate 29 (22.8%); lamina papyracea, orbit or skull base 10 (7.9%); counts per site, overlapping. Editors' Wilson 95% intervals treating the 127 as one sample, which overstates precision because the series were selected and differ: 95.7–99.9%, 50.4–67.2%, 22.6–38.4%, 16.4–30.9%, 4.3–13.9%. Series selecting a subgroup 12 of 17 (75 of 127 people); one group's three series 53 of 127 (editors' counts from Table 2). External nose (Table 5; 10 of 17 series): saddle nose 7 people in 5 series; nasal pyramid collapse 7 people in 2 series (editors' count). Use status known for 33 people: 18 using, 15 stopped (editors' count from Table 3); duration reported for 11 series (2–30 years), frequency for 2. Trimarchi et al. (2001), imaging at presentation, 16 of 18 people with lesions against 16 of 21 with Wegener granulomatosis (Table 3): septum 16 against 2; inferior turbinate 12 (both sides 9) against 0; middle turbinate 10 (both sides 5) against 0; superior turbinates 2; lateral nasal wall 5 (lamina papyracea 1); hard palate 4 (soft palate 1); 0 for each of these in the comparison group; second structure besides the septum 12 of 16 (75%) against 0 of 16; mean imaging score 4.06 (range 1–10) against 0.13 (0–1), p < 0.001. Figure 3 prints 61%, 33%, 16%, 11% and 28% for the inferior, middle and superior turbinates, the lateral wall and the floor or palate, which match neither. Palatal perforations 2 at the first visit, 5 by the end of follow-up (12–108 months, median 34). During follow-up: orbital infections 2, lung abscess 1, all resolved with antibiotics; S. aureus in the nose 15 of 17. Presentation, lesions against vasculitis (Table 1): fever 0 against 13; weight loss 0 against 7; arthralgia or arthritis 0 against 7; lung involvement 0 against 12; ear involvement 0 against 7; CRP 12.2 (SD 12) against 79.4 (73.7) mg/L, p = 0.002; ESR 31 (25) against 66 (41) mm/h, p = 0.009; abnormal CRP 9 of 18, ESR 8 of 18. Routine ANCA positive 13 of 18 against 19 of 21. Biopsies (Table 4): giant cells or granulomas 0 of 25 against 9 of 22; deep necrosis 0 of 25 against 19 of 22 (both p < 0.001); leukocytoclastic vasculitis 7 of 25 against 14 of 22 biopsies (p = 0.02), 6 of 18 against 9 of 21 people (printed p = 0.11; editors' Fisher exact p = 0.74). Repeat imaging: 4 people, 8 further examinations 7–52 months after the first, all still using, all progressed. Saibene et al. (2025), 18 panellists, ratings from 1 to 9 (mean; median; range; outliers; result): 1.1 definition 7.44; 7.5; 1–9; 1; consensus. 1.3 not relying on autoantibody tests 8.50; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.3 differential diagnoses 8.50; 9; 6–9; 1; consensus. 3.3 stopping the only known way to halt lesions 8.61; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 3.4 no safe threshold 8.89; 9; 8–9; 0; strong consensus. 4.7 repair only after toxicology-proven stopping covering at least 12 months 8.61; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus. 4.8 reconstruction techniques 7.94; 9; 4–9; 2; near-consensus. 3.15 palatal obturator first 8.11; 9; 3–9; 1; consensus. 2.13 full workup if lesions grow after reported stopping 8.56; 9; 7–9; 0; strong consensus. 2.14 drug test then 8.22; 9; 5–9; 1; consensus.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive claim (which structures were damaged in people already diagnosed, how the damage was told apart from a vasculitis in one series, what has and has not been studied about its course, and what one expert panel recommends): observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low (the arithmetic floors at very low); descriptive claims are never upgraded. The certainty concerns the description of published cases. It does not extend to how often snorting cocaine damages the nose, which no paper read measured, or to healing after stopping, which no paper read studied. The panel's statements on stopping, the 'safe threshold' and the 12-month wait before repair are opinion (a consensus without patient data, its search excluding the primary case series) and are reported as such; resting on them alone, the claim would stay at draft. Status replicated: septal perforation in nearly every person is reported in each of the 17 series, by 14 different first authors (review Tables 2 and 3); but the shares come from one review whose pool includes the Brescia series and two later series from the same group, so they are not independently replicated, and the comparison with Wegener granulomatosis and the repeat imaging rest on one series. The review and the consensus share their first and senior authors and are not independent of each other. The claim gives no advice on use; amounts that people reported in the Brescia series are left out because no paper related them to the damage.

lines.q: What does snorting coke do to your nose, and does it heal?
lines.short: It can make a hole in the wall between your nostrils, and damage can spread. 126 of 127 people with this damage had that hole. Healing after stopping hasn't been studied.
lines.but: These are people who already had damage and went to doctors. Nobody knows how many people who snort get it.
how: 17 published case series held 127 people with this damage. 126 had a hole in the septum, the wall between the nostrils. Fewer had damage further in: about 59 in 100 on the lower side walls, 30 in 100 in the roof of the mouth, 23 in 100 higher up, 8 in 100 at the eye socket or skull base.

It can look like a disease that inflames blood vessels. In one Italian clinic, a blood test for that disease was positive in 13 of 18 people with cocaine damage, and some were first treated for that disease, which didn't help. Unlike many with that disease, none of the 18 had fever or illness elsewhere in the body.

None of these studies followed people after they stopped. In the Italian clinic, 4 people were scanned again months or years later. All 4 had kept using cocaine, and all had more damage. In one, it reached the base of the skull within three years.

18 nose doctors agreed, as opinion, that stopping is the only known way to halt the damage. They said no amount of use is safe for it. They'd wait for drug tests showing 12 months off cocaine before repair surgery.

lines.statement: In US Medicaid enrollees aged 18 to 64 who stopped buprenorphine after 6 to 18 months of continuous treatment and stayed enrolled for the next 6 months, about 5 in 100 had at least one medically treated drug overdose, and between 4 and 5 in 10 visited an emergency department, in the 6 months after stopping, in one claims-based cohort study with no group that stayed on treatment (Williams et al., 2020, read from the online-first version). In the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims of 2013–2017, 8,996 people met these conditions (61.0% women, 91.5% White, 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day). Stopping meant a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out, and the 6 months were counted from the last day of supply. In those 6 months, 464 people (5.2%; 95% CI 4.7 to 5.6, editors' calculation) had at least one medically treated overdose, opioid or non-opioid (5.1% to 5.5% in the four groups by length of treatment; 5.6% among the 8,077 with a recorded diagnosis of opioid use disorder); 41.2% to 48.6% had at least one emergency department visit, 11.3% to 13.9% at least one hospital admission, and 19.1% to 25.9% filled a prescription for a full-agonist opioid, which the authors read as a marker of relapse or poorly coordinated care. Against people treated for 6 to 9 months (4,126), those treated for 15 to 18 months (931) had lower adjusted odds of emergency visits (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.86), hospital admission (0.79, 0.64 to 0.99) and opioid prescriptions (0.67, 0.56 to 0.80), and those treated for 12 to 15 months lower odds of emergency visits (0.84) and opioid prescriptions (0.84), but the odds of overdose did not differ (15 to 18 months 1.04, 0.75 to 1.44, an interval that allows odds about 25% lower to 44% higher, editors' reading). Overdose after stopping was more likely with a recorded psychiatric diagnosis (odds ratio 1.61), alcohol use disorder (2.02) or another drug use disorder (1.51), and less likely in women (0.65). Because no group continued buprenorphine, the study cannot say whether stopping raised these risks compared with staying on treatment; the records do not say why anyone stopped; and the comparison of durations is adjusted only for age, sex, race, plan type, recorded diagnoses and starting dose, which the authors say leaves residual confounding possible. Deaths are not recorded: anyone who died, or lost Medicaid for any other reason, in the 6 months after stopping was excluded (3,940 of the 12,936 who stopped within the study window, 30.5%, editors' calculation), so fatal overdoses are not counted, as the authors say, and the figures are not the full risk after stopping. Only overdoses billed to Medicaid were counted, and the code list is printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50, which leaves out T40.0 to T40.4, the codes for poisoning by opium, heroin, methadone and other opioids (study card note), although the same sentence says that opioid overdoses were counted; the codes used are in an online table (S1) that was not on file. The people studied had all stayed in treatment at least 6 months, a minority the authors describe as likely relatively stable, so the figures may not apply to people who stop in the first weeks or months, or outside Medicaid. The discussion's statement that overdose rates after stopping are two to three times those of a general sample of people with opioid use disorder gives no figures and sets this study's medically treated overdoses beside death rates from another study, so it is not used here. Death rates during and after methadone or buprenorphine treatment, from a review of cohort studies, are a separate answer (see the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Adults aged 18 to 64 in the MarketScan multistate Medicaid claims database (2013–2017; contributing states not named) who began a new buprenorphine episode for opioid use disorder, stayed on it continuously for 6 to 18 months, then stopped, and stayed enrolled in Medicaid for the 6 months afterwards: 8,996 people (61.0% women; 91.5% White; 76.4% aged 25 to 44; mean starting dose 8.0 mg a day); people also covered by Medicare were excluded
lines.exposure: Stopping buprenorphine (a gap of more than 60 days after the last prescription's supply ran out) after 6–9 (4,126 people), 9–12 (2,440), 12–15 (1,499) or 15–18 months (931) of continuous treatment, by days supplied in pharmacy claims; the 6 months of follow-up counted from the last day of supply
lines.comparator: No group that continued buprenorphine. The longer-treatment groups against the 6–9-month group, adjusted for age, sex, race (White or not), Medicaid plan type, recorded psychiatric, alcohol and other drug use disorder diagnoses, and starting dose
lines.outcome: At least one medically treated drug overdose, opioid or non-opioid (ICD-10 codes printed as T36–T39 and T40.5–T50), at least one emergency department visit, at least one inpatient admission, and at least one filled full-agonist opioid prescription, in Medicaid claims in the 6 months after stopping; deaths not recorded
lines.magnitude: Williams et al. (2020). Flow: 26,576 with a new continuous episode of more than 6 months; 10,481 who did not stop (39.4%, editors) and 3,159 who stopped too late in the study window removed; 12,936 who stopped within the window; 3,940 (30.5%, editors) removed for incomplete enrolment in the 6 months after stopping; 8,996 analysed (6–9 months 4,126; 9–12 months 2,440; 12–15 months 1,499; 15–18 months 931). Six-month outcomes across the four groups, unadjusted: emergency department visit 41.2–48.6% (abstract 42.1–49.9%), inpatient admission 11.3–13.9%, full-agonist opioid prescription 19.1–25.9%, medically treated overdose 5.1–5.5%; overall overdose 464/8,996 = 5.2% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–5.6, editors). 15–18 against 6–9 months, unadjusted: emergency visits 41.2% against 48.6% (p < 0.001), admissions 11.3% against 13.9% (p < 0.05), opioid prescriptions 19.1% against 25.9% (p < 0.001). Adjusted odds ratios against 6–9 months (Table 2): 15–18 months, admission 0.79 (0.64–0.99), emergency visit 0.75 (0.65–0.86), overdose 1.04 (0.75–1.44), opioid prescription 0.67 (0.56–0.80); 12–15 months 0.86 (0.72–1.03), 0.84 (0.75–0.95), 1.10 (0.84–1.43), 0.84 (0.73–0.97); 9–12 months 0.86 (0.74–1.01), 0.94 (0.85–1.04), 1.04 (0.82–1.30), 0.95 (0.85–1.07). Overdose, other terms in the same model: women 0.65 (0.54–0.79); psychiatric diagnosis 1.61 (1.32–1.96); alcohol use disorder 2.02 (1.47–2.79); non-opioid drug use disorder 1.51 (1.22–1.86); starting dose 1.00 per mg (0.97–1.04). Sensitivity analysis (8,077 with a recorded opioid use disorder diagnosis): 15–18 against 6–9 months, emergency visits 0.74 (0.64–0.86), admissions 0.79 (0.63–0.99), opioid prescriptions 0.68 (0.56–0.82); odds of overdose equivalent across groups, 5.6% overall.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive (how many people had each event in the 6 months after stopping): starts low; down one level for risk of bias, because exclusions that include every death and an overdose definition that cannot be checked could change the figures materially: very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. The comparisons by length of treatment are associations in the same records, open to confounding by why and when people stopped, and are not rated separately; the authors concede the design cannot show cause. Nothing here compares stopping with continuing: deaths during and after treatment are the subject of the answer on whether it is dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine, which rests on a review of cohort studies and measures deaths, not treated overdoses; the two do not conflict. Status: single study.

lines.short: In US records, about 5 in 100 people had an overdose treated by a doctor within 6 months of stopping. Nearly half went to an emergency department.
lines.but: People who died were left out, so fatal overdoses aren't counted. And nobody stayed on Suboxone to compare with.
how: US public health insurance (Medicaid) records tracked 8,996 people for 6 months after they stopped Suboxone's main drug, buprenorphine. They'd been on it for 6 to 18 months.

464 had at least one overdose treated by a doctor (5 in 100). 41 to 49 in 100 went to an emergency department, 11 to 14 in 100 stayed in hospital and 19 to 26 in 100 filled a prescription for another opioid.
People who'd been on it 15 to 18 months had fewer emergency visits, hospital stays and opioid prescriptions afterwards than those who stopped at 6 to 9 months. Their overdoses were no fewer.
Anyone who died or lost Medicaid in those 6 months was left out, and the records don't say why people stopped. Deaths during and after treatment are in a separate answer.

lines.statement: How long a drug can still be found by a test after it was last taken is known only roughly. In two narrative reviews, the usual detection times are second-hand figures from single small studies, or from textbooks and laboratory web pages, and the one primary study read that watched people stop (cannabis) could not see when many of them would have turned negative. The first review (Verstraete, 2004, a single-author summary with no stated search) puts one 'typical' study in each cell of its tables for blood, urine and oral fluid, mostly a single controlled dose given to volunteers, in many studies at doses the author calls low compared with street doses and in some to only one or two people, measured as far as possible down to the method's limit of detection rather than at screening cutoffs (some rows use cutoffs), and for several drugs takes the longest times from people who stopped heavy use in prison or on a detoxification ward. From these it summarizes that after a single dose most drugs could be detected in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 or 2 days and in oral fluid for 5 to 48 hours, and after chronic use in urine for about a week after last use, longer in extreme cases (benzoylecgonine, a breakdown product of cocaine, 22 days after last use in people using cocaine heavily; cannabis up to about 3 months, the longest reports, 93 and 95 days, being called probably exceptional); hair holds drugs longest, depending on its length, with few data on single doses. It calls detection times extremely variable: they depend on the amount, the route, acute or chronic use, the fluid tested, the test's limit or cutoff, the substance sought and differences between people. In one study it cites, urine was last positive after a single controlled dose of methamphetamine at 87 hours on average (46 to 144) at the method's limit of quantification but at 43 hours (22 to 65) at cutoffs of 500 ng/mL methamphetamine and 200 ng/mL amphetamine. After heavy use, times ran longer than the single-dose figures: in a series of 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 88.4% still screened positive for morphine after 1 day and 44.8% after 6 days (the review gives neither the numbers tested each day nor when the days start), and in 18 people housed on a closed research unit, the last positive cocaine screen came on average 81 hours (34 to 162) after the last use they reported. The second review (Moeller et al., 2017, a clinical review for clinicians) gives a table of 'approximate' urine detection times, adapted from the authors' 2008 review, with no cutoff, test, amount or conditions for any value (for example cocaine metabolites 2 to 4 days; heroin, as morphine, 48 hours; amphetamine and methamphetamine 48 hours; diazepam 30 days and lorazepam 3 days; cannabis 3 days after a single use, 5 to 7 days with use 4 times a week, 10 to 15 days with daily use and more than 30 days in a chronic heavy smoker); its nine sources are a 1987 report, a pain-medicine review, a textbook, the 2008 review, two laboratory web pages, a psychiatry textbook chapter, the 2004 review and a pharmacists' newsletter. It adds that a result below the cutoff is reported as negative, which means the level was below the cutoff, not that the drug was absent, and that the heroin-specific breakdown product 6-acetylmorphine shows in urine only up to about 8 hours. In the one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008), 60 adults in the USA who reported cannabis dependence or abuse and regular smoking (on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days) lived on a closed research unit under 24-hour medical surveillance with random drug tests for up to 30 days, and every urine sample was screened by immunoassay at the US federal workplace cutoff of 50 ng/mL; days since last use before admission were not reported, so every time runs from admission. The last positive screen came 0 to 29.8 days after admission, on average 4.6, 9.7 and 15.4 days in the groups whose first sample held the least, middling and most THCCOOH, the breakdown product tested for (relative to creatinine: up to 50, 51 to 150 and above 150 ng/mg; 19, 21 and 20 people). These averages are minimums: 13 of the 20 in the highest group were still screening positive on their last day of observation (on average day 19; for 4 of them day 30), and of the 16 people watched for 27 days or more, 6, all in the highest group, were still positive when watching ended (editors' count from Table II). Six of the 60 never screened positive on the unit, and in 43 of the 46 people who had both negative and positive screens a positive came after the first negative (editors' count), the pattern of positive, negative and positive again that the authors describe as levels fall. None of these sources gives the detection time for a particular person, amount or test. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People tested for drugs after use: in the studies summarized second-hand by two narrative reviews, mostly healthy volunteers given a single controlled dose (some studies of one or two people) and people who stopped regular use in prison, on a detoxification ward or on a closed research unit; in the one primary study read, 60 adults aged 18 to 45 in the USA (46 men, 14 women; 50 African American; mean age 26.9) who reported cannabis dependence or abuse (DSM-IV terms) and smoking on average 9.4 joints a week on 10.6 of the last 14 days, kept abstinent on a closed research unit
lines.exposure: Last use of a drug, as a single controlled dose given by researchers or as the end of regular use (in prison, on a detoxification ward or on admission to a closed research unit), followed by tests of urine, blood, oral fluid or hair; in the primary study, cannabis smoked before admission (amounts and THC content unknown; days since last use not reported), then enforced abstinence for up to 30 days
lines.comparator: None: detection times are described, not compared with a control group; in some reviewed studies the same samples were read at different limits or cutoffs; in the primary study, groups formed by the THCCOOH/creatinine of the first urine sample
lines.outcome: Detection time: how long after a single dose, after last reported use or after admission a drug or its breakdown product was found above the stated detection limit or cutoff; in the primary study, days from admission to the first negative and to the last positive urine screen at 50 ng/mL, and whether people were still screening positive when observation ended
lines.magnitude: Verstraete (2004), as summarized (pp. 200, 204): single dose, urine 1.5–4 days, blood 1–2 days, oral fluid 5–48 hours (low ng/mL level); chronic use, urine about 1 week after last use; extreme cases cocaine 22 days, cannabis up to 3 months (longest reports 93 and 95 days, called probably exceptional). Table 2, typical urine times, one study per row (study conditions): methamphetamine 87 ± 51 h (2.5 ng/mL), maximal 6 days; MDMA 48 h (20 ng/mL); cannabis 34 h and 87 h after one cigarette (THCCOOH 15 ng/mL; text 33.7 ± 9.2 and 88.6 ± 9.5 h), maximal 95 days; cocaine 48–72 h (benzoylecgonine 1000 ng/mL), maximal 22 days; LSD 36 h, 2-oxo-3-hydroxy-LSD 96 h (0.2 ng/mL), maximal 4 days; heroin as morphine 11–54 h (no limit given), maximal 11.3 days; GHB 12 h (10,000 ng/mL); amphetamine maximal 9 days. Methamphetamine after one controlled dose, last detection: 87.2 ± 51 h (46–144) at 2.5 ng/mL; 51.6 ± 26.3 h (25–77) at 250 and 100 ng/mL; 42.7 ± 22.8 h (22–65) at 500 and 200 ng/mL (methamphetamine and amphetamine). Heroin: 63 men, morphine by immunoassay positive in 88.4%, 74.2%, 64.2%, 57.1%, 63.3% and 44.8% after 1 to 6 days (numbers per day not given); detoxification ward (52 people), total morphine (LOD 25 ng/mL) 4.95 days on average, at most 11.3; 6-acetylmorphine 5 h on average, at most 34.5 h. Cocaine: 18 people on a closed unit, immunoassay cutoff 300 ng/mL, last positive 57.5 ± 31.6 h (11–147) after admission and 81 ± 34 h (34–162) after last reported use. Cannabis, detoxification ward: urine THCCOOH (LOD 10 ng/mL) 4.9 days on average, at most 18. Moeller et al. (2017), Table 2 ('approximate'; no cutoff, test, amount or conditions): alcohol 7–12 h; amphetamine 48 h; methamphetamine 48 h; barbiturates short-acting 24 h, long-acting 3 weeks; benzodiazepines short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2–4 days; marijuana single use 3 days, 4 times a week 5–7 days, daily 10–15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 h; heroin (morphine) 48 h; hydromorphone 2–4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48–72 h; oxycodone 2–4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids single use 72 h, chronic more than 72 h; synthetic cathinones variable. Text: cannabis more than 30 days after stopping in chronic use, up to 72 h after a single exposure in people who do not use it; 6-acetylmorphine up to 8 h; ethyl glucuronide (alcohol) 2–5 days. Goodwin et al. (2008), 60 people, screen 50 ng/mL, days from admission, mean ± SD by first-sample THCCOOH/creatinine 0–50 (n = 19), 51–150 (n = 21) and above 150 ng/mg (n = 20): first negative 0.6 ± 0.8, 3.2 ± 2.8, 4.7 ± 4.8; last positive 4.6 ± 5.6 (abstract 4.3; 4.55 from the 13 individual values, editors' calculation), 9.7 ± 6.4, 15.4 ± 9.8; ranges 0.0–16.1 (first negative) and 0.0–29.8 (last positive). Still positive on the last day of observation: 13 of 20 in the highest group (mean last day 19; 4 on day 30); by the editors' count with the rule that reproduces these figures, 4 of 19 and 5 of 21 in the other groups (the Discussion says 2 in the lowest), 22 of the 54 who ever screened positive. Observed 27 days or more: 16, of whom 6 still positive at the end (last positives 27.3–29.8 days). Never positive on the unit: 6 of 60. A positive after the first negative: 43 of the 46 with both (42 of 45 without the impossible row F) (editors' counts from Table II).
lines.reasoning: Detection times are rated as descriptions (METHODS §6.3): the controlled-dose studies behind the reviews have no comparison group, and the primary study is a case series; start low. Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 (see the domain notes) take it to very low, the floor. The figures from the two narrative reviews are second-hand and the statement says so; the 2004 review reports the numbers of the primary studies it summarizes, which is the only way they are seen here. The one primary study read (Goodwin et al., 2008) is the strongest evidence for cannabis because abstinence was enforced, so later positive screens reflect what was left in the body, not new use; but it cannot give detection times from last use, and its averages are minimums. Status replicated: the direction (days after a single dose; longer, up to weeks, after heavy regular use, most of all for cannabis) agrees across separate studies described in the reviews (for cannabis, single-cigarette studies and a detoxification ward of 52 people) and the primary study; but every specific figure rests on one study, and only one primary study was read. Nothing is phrased as advice on avoiding or passing a test; the clinical review's section on tampering with samples was not used.

lines.q: How long do drugs show up on a drug test?
lines.short: It varies a lot. An expert review says most drugs show in urine for 1.5 to 4 days after one use. In one study, some regular weed smokers were still positive on day 30.
lines.but: The usual figures come from tiny studies. Some had just one or two people, given one dose in a lab.
how: One expert review sums up: after one use, most drugs showed in urine for 1.5 to 4 days, in blood for 1 to 2 days and in saliva for up to 2 days.

Each figure came from one small study, often measured to a lab's lowest limit. Another chart came from textbooks, older reviews and lab websites. The limit matters: one dose of meth showed for 87 hours at a lab's limit, 43 at a higher cutoff.
Heavy use can last longer than charts say. Among 63 men described as dependent on heroin, 45 in 100 still tested positive for morphine after 6 days. One chart lists 2 days for heroin.

On a locked ward where nobody could smoke, 60 regular weed smokers were tested for up to 30 days. 13 of the 20 with the highest levels were still positive when testing ended. Positives often came back after a negative.

lines.statement: In dried cannabis flower that licensed growers sent for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in six US states (Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington; December 2013 to January 2021; 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results), the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category that one consumer cannabis website's strain database links to each strain name, matched by name to the growers' own sample names (so the category is the website's, not necessarily what each package said; 73.4% of samples could be given one), was barely related to the samples' terpene profiles, the mix of the compounds the authors describe as responsible for cannabis's smell (Smith et al., 2022). THC and CBD content were not compared between the categories, and no effects on people were measured. Almost all samples were THC-dominant (at least five times as much THC as CBD): 96.5% overall and, by state, from 93.6% in Florida to 97.3% in Washington (editors' calculation from the counts in the paper's supporting figure S2, whose state totals match its Table 3 and whose THC-dominant total, 86,740, matches its Fig 1; the two figures disagree on how the other 3,183 samples split between balanced THC:CBD and CBD-dominant, 2,192 and 991 against 1,940 and 1,243, so no split is given here). In the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results, a score of how much more samples resemble others with the same label than samples with the nearest other label (the silhouette score, from −1 to 1) averaged −0.03 for the categories, with most samples below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their most abundant terpene and 0.38 for three groups found by a clustering method in the same terpene data, which the authors expected to separate better; the category analysis also counted 12,322 samples (29.9%) that had no category as a group of their own. Strain names carried more information: for 26 of the 41 names attached to at least five growers with at least five samples each, products sold under the same name by different growers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random, 13 did not differ from chance and 2 (LSD and Durban Poison) were less alike than chance (editors' count of the significance marks in the paper's figure); even randomly paired products were fairly similar, at about 0.69 on a 0-to-1 similarity scale (read from the figure). Among 12,063 THC-dominant products with a category, Sativa products made up 30.9% of the terpinolene-rich group against 15.0% overall, yet that group was still mostly Hybrid (55.8%), and the test the paper reports for this appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts (editors' calculation). The six laboratories' methods were not standardized, which the authors say prevents them from separating laboratory from regional differences, and the corresponding author is employed by the website that supplied the categories and strain names. In a small Dutch study, two cultivars that a seed company's website describes as Sativa-dominant (Amnesia) and Indica-dominant (White Widow), bought at ten coffee shops in four cities on two visits about two months apart (35 samples), differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but had similar THC (about 17% and 16% of the weight); many compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases of the same name, 3 samples had the chemistry of the other cultivar and were left out as presumed mix-ups, and of three pharmacy varieties one, bred from a variety with a large share of Sativa genes, resembled the Indica-dominant cultivar (Hazekamp & Fischedick, 2012; no statistical tests of these differences; the first author worked for the grower of the pharmacy varieties). Neither study measured how the products felt, so neither can say whether the labels predict effects. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
lines.exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
lines.comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
lines.outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured
lines.magnitude: Smith et al. (2022), chemotypes (THC:CBD 5:1 or more THC-dominant, 1:5 or less CBD-dominant, balanced between): 86,740 of 89,923 samples THC-dominant (96.5%; Fig 1 and the sum of S2 Fig agree); by state (S2 Fig legends; THC-dominant, balanced, CBD-dominant; totals as in Table 3): Alaska 6,049, 179, 25; California 7,801, 174, 137; Florida 1,517, 57, 46; Michigan 6,932, 183, 125; Oregon 12,692, 505, 311; Washington 51,749, 1,094, 347; THC-dominant share 96.7%, 96.2%, 93.6%, 95.7%, 94.0% and 97.3% (editors' calculation); balanced and CBD-dominant 2,192 and 991 by S2 Fig against 1,940 and 1,243 in Fig 1 (text: 2.2% and 1.4%), a disagreement the paper does not explain. THC-dominant samples with terpene results (n = 41,201): mean silhouette score −0.03 for the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (groups: Hybrid 17,616, no category 12,322, Indica 6,681, Sativa 4,582), 0.27 for the dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters; differences |d′| = 3.49 (k-means against category), 1.83 (dominant terpene against category) and 0.54 (k-means against dominant terpene), all P < 0.0001; no intervals. Clusters: I (caryophyllene-limonene) 21,811 (52.9%), II (myrcene-pinene) 14,188 (34.4%), III (terpinolene-myrcene) 5,202 (12.6%). Strain names (41): more consistent than shuffled names for 26, no different for 13, less consistent for 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) (editors' count of the Fig 8C significance marks; the text gives one test for the majority of names, P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed); shuffled baseline about 0.69 cosine similarity (read from Fig 8C); Purple Punch 96% of products in one cluster against 61.8% expected under shuffling, Tangie 62.5% in its most common cluster. Category shares among 12,063 products with a category (editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III Hybrid 55.8%, Indica 13.3%, Sativa 30.9% (χ² 22.2, P < 0.0001 as printed); editors' calculation: the χ² formula applied to the Fig 9B percentages as if they were counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III and 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, which the paper reports as not different. Hazekamp & Fischedick (2012): THC 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88) in Amnesia against 159.5 (SD 26.76) in White Widow, reported as not significantly different with no test shown; myrcene 0.7 against 2.9 mg/g; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia, not detected in White Widow; relative standard deviation above 25% for 14 compounds as printed (editors' count of Table 1: 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds); 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other cultivar.
lines.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read. The US paper's supporting figures, read in round pdf-2026-11-26, add the THC-dominant share in each state and a disagreement between two of its figures about the other samples; they do not change the rating.

lines.q: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed?
lines.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
lines.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed made people feel.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples from licensed growers in six US states, 2013 to 2021. In every state, 94 to 97 in 100 samples had at least five times as much THC as CBD. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name, and weren't compared on THC or CBD.

In 41,201 samples where THC outweighed CBD, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.
